paras: The killing of Archie Stokes at the Woodlawn road convict camp took place on the morning of March 24, 1888, near Birmingham, Alabama, when deputy sheriffs fired on a squad of leased county convicts who had refused to work. Stokes, a Black convict, was killed and a second convict, Henry Allen, was wounded, and a coroner's jury found the shooting was done in performance of duty. Papers around the country carried the story as the suppression of a convict "mutiny".

According to a special dispatch to the Memphis Appeal, the county commissioners had some months earlier barred the whipping of any convict except on the order and in the presence of the county engineer and warden. The dispatch claimed that the convicts had since been so "defiant of authority" that the road contractors who leased them could barely cover expenses. A squad of twenty-five worked by contractor J. M. Lovelace on the Woodlawn road, some four miles from the city, was described as especially troublesome.

On the morning of March 24 the squad announced it would not work any more, and Lovelace went to town for two deputy sheriffs. Probate Judge Porter and Sheriff Truss directed the deputies to "suppress the mutiny one way or another" and return the men to work. When the officers arrived, the convicts withdrew into their shanty and warned that anyone who interfered would do so at his peril.

The deputies summoned a posse of citizens, tore a board from the side of the shanty and fired in among the convicts. Stokes ran out with a pick and made at one of the posse, and he was killed instantly by a volley of pistol and gunshot. Allen had been wounded in the side by one of the first shots.

A coroner's jury returned a verdict that the shooting was done in the performance of duty. No report of any further inquiry, of charges against the officers, or of what became of Allen or the rest of the squad appears in the coverage.

The fullest account was a Birmingham special to the Memphis Appeal, printed March 25 under "Alabama Convicts Killed. Mutinous State Prisoners Shot By Deputy Sheriffs Near Birmingham." A version dated March 26 ran in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer under "Deputies Use Their Guns and Restore Order After Killing a Negro" and in Ohio and Kentucky papers as "Mutiny Quelled" and "Suppressing a Rebellion". These reprints called the convicts "rebels" and placed the camp "forty miles" from the city, and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union reduced the story to one line reporting that two mutinous convicts had been killed by officers.
A second, shorter Birmingham dispatch dated March 25 ran in the Anderson Intelligencer and, condensed, in The Gale on April 7. Every version gave the officers' account, and none quoted a convict.

The two dispatches differ on how the shooting began. In the wire story the whole squad held out in the shanty and the deputies and a posse fired in first, while the March 25 dispatch says only Stokes and Allen refused, keeping the others in the barracks and standing in the door "armed with picks" until two deputies opened fire. The second dispatch also mentions no posse, calls Allen "severely wounded" though not fatally, and names the camp "Loveless".

reader.title: Killing of Archie Stokes at the Woodlawn road convict camp
bases: Two deputy sheriffs, sent to put mutinous leased convicts back to work, summoned a posse of citizens and fired into the convicts' shanty, killing Archie Stokes (A1, A2); a second dispatch names only the deputies (A4).

Stokes was killed by two deputy sheriffs and a summoned posse acting on the orders of the sheriff and probate judge, and a coroner's jury found the shooting was done in performance of duty (A1, A2); the killing was an act of officers enforcing custody and labor discipline, not extralegal punishment, though the account comes from the officers' side (A1, A4).

Two separately worded Birmingham dispatches agree that deputies shot and killed the convict Archie Stokes and wounded Henry Allen after the convicts refused to work (A1, A4), though they differ on details and one brief says two convicts were killed (A3).

accounts.label: Wire report (Birmingham special, March 24/26)
accounts.gist: The whole squad of twenty-five refused to work after the county barred whipping; deputies and a citizens' posse tore a board off the shanty and fired in, and Stokes was killed when he ran out with a pick.

accounts.label: Second Birmingham dispatch (March 25)
accounts.gist: Only Stokes and Allen refused, holding the others in the barracks and defying the guards with picks; two deputies opened fire and shot Stokes as he rushed at them.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Found the shooting was done in performance of duty.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal's headline called the men 'Mutinous State Prisoners' and the dispatch blamed their defiance on the county's ban on whipping, calling them 'the rebels'.
Northern and border papers ran the wire story under 'Deputies Use Their Guns and Restore Order After Killing a Negro', 'Mutiny Quelled' and 'Suppressing a Rebellion'.
The Anderson Intelligencer and The Gale ran the shorter second dispatch without headline comment among regional news.
